raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis C virus coinfection presented with an atypical pharyngeal lesion. He had a history of intravenous drug use and cigarette smoking. He had recently recorded a CD4+ T-cell count nadir below 100 cells/muL due to self-cessation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Three months prior to the lesion appearing, he had been recommenced ART, which included emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir.
A small plaque-like lesion was first noted near his right lower wisdom tooth. As the lesion resembled oral hairy leukoplakia, he was treated with courses of valaciclovir and aciclovir while the lesion relapsed and remitted. After four months, his CD4+ T-cell count had risen to 340 cells/muL and HIV replication was fully suppressed, but this was accompanied by growth of the thick, white, well-circumscribed, exophytic plaque to cover the left tonsil, along with uvula enlargement, a change in voice quality, a dry cough, and bilateral otalgia. There was no lymphadenopathy nor systemic symptoms.
The patient had mild eosinophilia (0.46 x 109/L) with normal levels of other leucocytes. Syphilis serology was negative. A CT scan (Figure 1) demonstrated that the lesion extended from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx. He was commenced on amoxicillin/clavulanic acid orally with no change in the lesion. A left tonsillar biopsy was performed which was complicated by postoperative hemorrhage.
Microscopic examination (Figures 2(A), 2(B), 2(C), and 2(D)) of the tonsil revealed a dense inflammatory cell infiltrate consisting largely of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils. There was exocytosis of eosinophils into the overlying squamous mucosa and vascular proliferation comprising of numerous thin-walled capillary-sized vessels arranged in a lobular pattern. Foci of necrosis were present, some of which were centered around blood vessels, but there was no vasculitis. The B- and T-cell markers were of a benign mixed pattern, excluding a lymphoproliferative process.
The biopsy demonstrated a reactive process with unusual areas of necrosis, although no opportunistic infection was identified: no fungi were seen on the methenamine silver or periodic acid-Schiff stains; the Warthin-Starry stain for spirochetes was negative; no acid-fast bacilli were seen; and Cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and LMP1 for Epstein-Barr virus immunoperoxidase stains were negative. The vascular proliferation and eosinophilia were most consistent with angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia; however, the vessels lacked the classic cobblestone endothelial lining, and the location in the tonsil was not typical. The presence of eosinophilia, along with the clinical picture, distinguishes this from pyogenic granuloma, which is seen on the oral mucosa but is characterized by a classic red polypoid appearance.
Despite various treatments including antibiotics, antivirals, and surgical debridement, the lesion continued to wax and wane, but after 48 months, it resolved completely, possibly due to immune control.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old man with HIV and hepatitis C virus co-infection presented with a persistent, enlarging white exophytic tonsillar and oropharyngeal plaque, uvular swelling, voice change, dry cough, and bilateral otalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following self-cessation of antiretroviral therapy and a CD4+ nadir <100 cells/µL, the patient restarted ART (emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir) 3 months prior to first noticing a small plaque near his right lower third molar. Initially treated with courses of valaciclovir and aciclovir for presumed oral hairy leukoplakia with waxing and waning behavior, over the ensuing 4 months—coinciding with immune recovery to a CD4+ count of 340 cells/µL and full HIV viral suppression—the lesion expanded into a thick, white, well-circumscribed exophytic plaque covering the left tonsil with uvular enlargement, dysphonia, dry cough, and bilateral referred ear pain, unresponsive to oral amoxicillin/clavulanic acid.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV and hepatitis C virus co-infection; history of prior ART interruption with CD4+ nadir <100 cells/µL; history of intravenous drug use and cigarette smoking.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pharyngeal mass sensation, altered voice quality, dry cough, and bilateral otalgia; negative for fever, weight loss, or other constitutional symptoms. Home medications: emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir.

objective.physical_examination: Oropharyngeal examination revealed a thick, white, well-circumscribed exophytic plaque covering the left palatine tonsil accompanied by uvular enlargement, without cervical or generalized lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count showed mild eosinophilia (0.46 x 10^9/L) with normal remaining leukocyte subsets. Syphilis serology was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count had risen from a nadir of <100 cells/µL to 340 cells/µL. Neck CT demonstrated a mass lesion extending from the nasopharynx to the oropharynx. Left tonsillar biopsy (complicated by postoperative hemorrhage) demonstrated a dense reactive polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate of plasmacytoid lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils with mucosal eosinophilic exocytosis, lobular capillary-sized vascular proliferation (lacking cobblestone endothelium), and perivascular necrosis without vasculitis. B- and T-cell immunohistochemistry showed a benign polyclonal mixed pattern, and special stains/immunoperoxidase for GMS, PAS, Warthin-Starry (spirochetes), AFB, CMV, HSV, and EBV LMP1 were all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Atypical reactive angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia (ALHE)-like naso-oropharyngeal lesion associated with immune reconstitution following ART re-initiation in a 35-year-old male with HIV/HCV co-infection (suppressed HIV viral load and CD4+ T-cell recovery from <100 to 340 cells/µL on emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and ritonavir-boosted darunavir). Lymphoma, syphilis, fungal/mycobacterial infections, HSV, CMV, EBV oral hairy leukoplakia, and classic pyogenic granuloma were excluded via histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and negative special stains. Despite trials of oral antibiotics, antivirals, and surgical debridement, the lesion waxed and waned before achieving complete spontaneous resolution after 48 months of sustained immune control on ART.
